.pp-term p: HCI researcher who, with Shumin Zhai, derived the steering law in 1997 — how speed and error change when a pointer must travel a constrained path.
Appears in Steering Law
Psychologist at NYU Stern whose research with Daniel Oppenheimer showed how processing fluency shapes judgments, from stock prices to reasoning.
Appears in Processing Fluency

Computer scientist at Microsoft Research whose work on human-AI interaction produced the 2019 guidelines, distilled from two decades of scattered recommendations and tested against products people use daily.
Appears in Microsoft’s 18 AI Guidelines
Wired editor whose Long Tail argued the unpopular 80 percent becomes a market once serving it gets cheap.
Appears in Pareto Principle
Behavioral economist and author of Predictably Irrational whose experiments — including assembling IKEA boxes — showed how effort inflates the value of what we build.
Appears in IKEA Effect · Anchoring Effect
Newspaper design scholar who systematized reading gravity — how attention falls diagonally across an evenly weighted page.
Appears in Gutenberg Principle
Cognitive neuroscientist whose 2006 experiments with Maital Neta showed people prefer curved objects at a glance — sharp contours read as threat before thought begins.
Appears in Contour Bias
British psychologist whose 1983 paper Ironies of Automation showed that automating the easy parts of a job leaves an out-of-practice operator the hard ones.
Appears in Out-of-the-Loop Problem
UCLA information scientist who described berrypicking, the evolving, bit-by-bit way people actually search.
Appears in Cognitive Models of Information Retrieval
Social psychologist known for research on self-control and ego depletion, the theory behind decision fatigue.
Appears in Decision Fatigue
Information scientist who proposed the anomalous state of knowledge: people search because they sense a gap they can’t fully describe.
Appears in Cognitive Models of Information Retrieval
Information retrieval and machine learning researcher, for many years at Microsoft Research, working on ranking, personalization, and how people read what a system surfaces.
Appears in Microsoft’s 18 AI Guidelines
Usability researcher who, with David Lane at Rice University, ran the 1998 tests that named banner blindness.
Appears in Banner Blindness
Inventor of the web and founder of the W3C, whose line “the power of the web is in its universality” opens the accessibility case.
Appears in WCAG and POUR
Civil rights advocate and founder of PolicyLink whose 2017 essay The Curb-Cut Effect argued that changes designed for excluded groups end up benefiting everyone.
Appears in Curb Cut Effect
Software engineer who led the design of the Java Collections Framework, and whose 2006 talk How to Design a Good API and Why It Matters applies least astonishment to naming and behavior.
Appears in Principle of Least Astonishment
UX designer who coined the term dark patterns in 2010, built the pattern library now at deceptive.design, and wrote the book Deceptive Patterns (2023).
Appears in Dark Patterns
Canadian poet and typographer whose The Elements of Typographic Style (1992) set out the widely quoted guideline of 45 to 75 characters per line.
Appears in Line Length
Author of The Mythical Man-Month, who named Conway’s Law and gave software engineering its most quoted warnings.
Appears in Conway’s Law
Cognitive psychologist who co-founded the Harvard Center for Cognitive Studies with George Miller in 1960.
Appears in Miller’s Law
English writer whose 1929 parable of the fence became the engineering rule: understand it before you remove it.
Appears in Chesterton’s Fence
Xerox PARC researcher who helped found human-computer interaction as a science and, with Peter Pirolli, developed information foraging theory.
Appears in Cognitive Models of Information Retrieval
Information scientist whose training-wheels interfaces at IBM proved that hiding advanced functions helps novices learn.
Appears in Progressive Disclosure
Behavioral economist who co-coined the curse of knowledge in 1989 — better-informed people can’t ignore what they know.
Appears in Curse of Knowledge
Social scientist whose 1976 law described how quantitative indicators corrupt the processes they monitor.
Appears in Goodhart’s Law
Psychologist whose book Influence (1984) named social proof as one of six principles of persuasion, and whose field studies showed how descriptive norms change behavior.
Appears in Social Proof
User researcher at Microsoft, among the practitioners who tested the candidate guidelines against products people use every day.
Appears in Microsoft’s 18 AI Guidelines
Computer scientist whose 1968 observation that systems mirror the organizations that build them became Conway’s Law.
Appears in Conway’s Law
Psychologist who named flow — the state of full absorption when challenge and skill are matched.
Appears in Yerkes-Dodson Law
Psychologist who, with Robert Yerkes, showed in 1908 that performance peaks at moderate arousal and collapses past it.
Appears in Yerkes-Dodson Law

Appears in Doherty Threshold
Stanford psychologist known for research on mindsets, including evidence that beliefs about willpower shape whether people feel depleted.
Appears in Decision Fatigue
Founder of experimental memory research — the serial position effect, the forgetting curve, and the spacing effect all trace to his 1880s work.
Appears in Serial Position Effect · Ebbinghaus Illusion
Economist and military analyst whose 1961 paper on risk and ambiguity showed that people avoid unknown probabilities; later known for releasing the Pentagon Papers.
Appears in Ambiguity Effect
American engineer whose work on situation awareness, and the 1995 study with Esin Kiris, named the cost of supervising automation rather than doing the work.
Appears in Out-of-the-Loop Problem
Expertise researcher whose deliberate-practice work explains why not all repetitions bend the learning curve equally.
Appears in Power Law of Practice
Greek mathematician whose Elements, around 300 BC, defined the extreme and mean ratio — the golden ratio — two thousand years before it got its name.
Appears in Golden Ratio

Appears in Hook Model

Appears in Weber-Fechner Law
Air Force human-factors pioneer whose 1954 model of target acquisition still governs every button size and cursor path.

Stanford behavior scientist behind the B = M · A · P model and the Tiny Habits method.
Appears in Fogg Behavior Model
Principal researcher at Microsoft Research working on AI agents and the interfaces people use to direct them.

Appears in Gall’s Law
Writer who popularized — and flattened — Ericsson’s research into the 10,000-hours rule.

Appears in Goodhart’s Law

Inventor of the movable-type printing press, whose name the reading-gravity diagram borrowed five centuries later.

Design and research leader at Motorola, Microsoft, and Amazon, known for methods that surface articulated and latent customer needs; co-created UI Tenets and Traps.

Appears in Hick’s Law
Cognitive scientist and Pulitzer-winning author of Gödel, Escher, Bach — and of the recursive law about everything taking longer.

Microsoft Research scientist studying human-AI collaboration, and how people decide when a machine's judgment deserves their trust.
